extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism; educated English readers interested in George Sand and 19th-century French literature
extracted.subtask_description: A literary-critical essay outlining the central motives, themes, stylistic qualities, and social/religious ideas in George Sand's oeuvre, and advising how to approach and judge her work. The page aims to characterize her ruling thought and the evolution of her writing over forty years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impression of simplicity (manner and style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Madame Sand's prevailing impression is one of 'simplicity, frank, cordial simplicity' in manner and (by implication) in her writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic notes examples of simple and cordial behaviour (receiving a visitor, giving flowers, cordial handshakes) and recommends attending to that simplicity as a primary quality when judging her personality and tone in her works. Simplicity is presented as a central, positive trait rather than mere plainness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ruling thought / ground-motive: 'the sentiment of the ideal life'
rubrics_metrics.description: Her ruling thought is given by the phrase: 'Le sentiment de la vie idéale, qui n'est autre que la vie normale telle que nous sommes appelés à la connaître' — 'the sentiment of the ideal life, which is none other than man's normal life as we shall some day know it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'sentiment of the ideal life' is treated as the organizing motive of her entire strain; readers should interpret themes, character aims, and social ideas in light of this ideal of a future, normalized human life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cry of agony and revolt
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the three grand elements of her strain is the 'cry of agony and revolt' prevalent in her earlier works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify early-period emotional, declamatory, or rebellious passages (e.g., Lélia, Valentine) as expressions of this element; note its passion and the way it leaves an ineffaceable impression even if readers later cease to re-read those works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust in nature and beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: A principal element is a deep 'trust in nature and beauty' — nature as consoling, restorative, and central to human flourishing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate her close, faithful natural descriptions (wild-flowers named, lanes, meadows, peasant life) and passages that present nature as a source of healing and poetic satisfaction. Consider how nature moderates and consoles the earlier revolt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspiration for social renewal (renaissance sociale)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sustained aspiration toward a 'purged and renewed human society' — social equality, fraternity, and a social rebirth — is a central element of her work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit social/political declarations, advocacy of equality, and representations of peasant life as the seed of future civilization. Treat social idealism as integral to evaluating her themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evolution of themes across the author's career
rubrics_metrics.description: Over forty years her work evolves: the early 'cry of agony and revolt' gives way to a movement toward nature, beauty, and social renewal; elements appear in varying prominence at different times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a given work, situate it within this temporal development; do not treat early and late works as equivalent. Note which of the three grand elements dominates and how the author's motive unfolds with 'unfailing resolve' and 'absolute sincerity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Oeuvre unity / total-impression beyond single works or characters
rubrics_metrics.description: George Sand is more than the sum of charming stories or memorable characters; her 'spirit' goes through her work as a whole and must be felt across the corpus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid judging her solely by one popular novel (e.g., Consuelo) or by isolated characters; aim to apprehend the consistent motive and tone across representative works to form a 'powerful total-impression.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of representative works to grasp the spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: To feel her spirit it suffices to read a few well-chosen books rather than everything; the critic suggests Lettres d'un Voyageur, Mauprat, François le Champi, and Valvèdre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these titles as a minimal reading set to sample the three principal elements and the author's range. The list is prescriptive: these works 'contain all the principal elements of their author's strain.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Character creation: fidelity to nature and attractiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: She creates characters with 'admirable truth to nature'—attractive and attaching figures (e.g., Edmée, Geneviève, Germain)—but character-making is only part of her expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess characters for naturalness and emotional attachment; recognize that excellent character-drawing is one dimension but not the whole of her literary achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and cadences: grandeur and musical quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Her sentences possess 'grandiose and moving' cadences that linger in memory ('they haunt the ear with their cadences').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate stylistic features such as rhetorical sweep, cadence, lyricism, and memorable phrasing; these stylistic cadences are central to her effect (compared to Werther). Note also that some of this style may be seen as overwrought by some readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful, intimate depiction of rural nature and local detail
rubrics_metrics.description: She keeps readers 'closely and truly intimate with rural nature,' naming actual wild-flowers and rendering local Berry landscapes with loving precision (lanes, meadows, oxen, farmhouses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge passages for concreteness of natural detail, the authenticity of rural scene-painting (e.g., Holbein-influenced opening to La Mare au Diable), and the sensory specificity that resists facile translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peasant as central figure and socio-symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: The peasant is the central human figure in her work and symbolically represents 'France, life, the future' — the foundation for social health and renewal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine how peasants are depicted (probity, charity, self-respect, tact), their psychological and moral qualities, and their political/social role within Sand's vision. Treat peasant life as both subject-matter and ideological statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and beauty as instruments of social consolation and reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature is not merely aesthetic but is portrayed as a 'vast power of healing and delight for all' and as foundational to a better social order where 'mind, heart, and hands shall be alive together.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating, note passages that connect aesthetic appreciation with social prescriptions: nature's beauty as a lever for making life fruitful and for reordering labor and social harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit social-political doctrine: equality and fraternity
rubrics_metrics.description: She treats equality as a 'holy doctrine' and the 'goal of man and the law of the future,' investing political equality with religious and civilizational significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess political rhetoric and claims about national character (e.g., France as 'the nation which loves and is loved'), and weigh how strongly didactic or prophetic language shapes the work. Contextualize impassioned claims (e.g., post-1870) when judging tone and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious/mystical sensibility (divine sense, pantheism)
rubrics_metrics.description: She abandons dogmatic religion but retains a 'divine sense'—a pantheistic or mystical feeling akin to Wordsworth's 'a presence that disturbs me with the joy of animating thoughts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify non-dogmatic religious sentiment in the text: pantheistic language, mystical consolation, and a turn to a universal presence rather than institutional belief. This sensibility underpins moral and aesthetic claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional resonance and lasting memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Her early passionate works leave an 'ineffaceable' impression; sentences and cadences linger and 'haunt the ear.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge works not only for argument or plot but for their ability to create durable emotional impressions in readers and to supply memorable phrasing that endures beyond immediate reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity, resolve, and moral earnestness
rubrics_metrics.description: Her evolution and repeated advocacy are pursued 'with the most unfailing resolve, the most absolute sincerity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for authorial earnestness when evaluating persuasive force: sincerity strengthens both moral claims and the credibility of her imaginative projects; lack of disingenuousness is a positive criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential excesses of rhetoric and context-sensitive distaste
rubrics_metrics.description: Her passionate outbursts (e.g., claims about France and equality, harsh denunciations of other nations) may appear exaggerated or distasteful to some readers, especially English ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize anti-patterns: declamatory or hyperbolic passages should be judged with awareness of historical context (the trauma of 1870) and the difference between passionate conviction and persuasive solidity. Note when rhetoric undermines credibility for certain audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between artistic aim and social/political propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Her art seeks both aesthetic ends and social ends (education of the peasant, social equality); she regards nature and art as public goods rather than private appropriation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate works for the balance they strike between literary qualities (style, character, imagery) and explicit social didacticism; determine whether the social purpose enriches or overpowers the artistic execution.
